# 10 Essential Formats for Newsletters to Supercharge Your Growth in 2026

In a world of overflowing inboxes, the 'what' of your newsletter is only half the battle; the 'how' is what truly captivates and converts. The structure you choose, the format, is the silent driver of engagement, building reader habits and delivering value long before they read a single word. Sending the same generic email blast week after week leads to audience fatigue and dwindling open rates. To stand out, you need a strategic approach that matches your message to the right delivery vehicle.

This guide moves beyond generic advice to dissect 10 powerful formats for newsletters, providing a strategic blueprint for each. We are not just talking about what they are, but how to use them effectively to achieve specific business goals. Forget one-size-fits-all templates; we’ll explore distinct structures designed to educate, engage, update, and build community.

Inside, you will find a comprehensive breakdown for each format, including:

- When to Use It: The specific scenarios where each format excels.
- Ideal Structure: A clear, repeatable layout to follow.
- Actionable Tips: Practical advice for subject lines, calls-to-action (CTAs), and frequency.
- Workflow Automation: Step-by-step guidance on how to implement and automate every format using NotionSender, from capturing content in Notion to scheduling your campaigns.

Prepare to transform your email strategy from a simple broadcast into a relationship-building powerhouse. Let's dive into the formats that will get your newsletter opened, read, and valued.

## 1. Curated Digest/Round-up Newsletter

The curated digest is one of the most powerful and scalable formats for newsletters. It positions you as a trusted filter, saving your audience time by sifting through the noise to deliver only the most valuable content. Instead of creating everything from scratch, you aggregate, comment on, and organize information from various sources around a central theme.

This format excels at building a loyal, engaged audience. Readers come to rely on your newsletter as their primary source for industry updates, transforming your send into a can't-miss part of their routine. Newsletters like The Hustle and Morning Brew built massive audiences by perfecting this model, delivering sharp, digestible summaries of business and tech news.

### When to Use This Format

This format is ideal if your audience is composed of busy professionals who value efficiency. It works best when you want to establish authority in a niche without the heavy lift of creating long-form original content every week. It's also perfect for community-builders who want to share member-generated content or highlight industry wins.

### Implementation with NotionSender

A curated digest is a prime candidate for a streamlined Notion-based workflow.

- Content Capture: Use a web clipper to save articles, tweets, and resources directly into a Notion database. Create a "Status" property (e.g., To Review, Approved, Published) to track each piece of content.
- Templating: Design a reusable template within your NotionSender database. This template should have placeholders for the link, a brief summary, and your personal commentary.
- Automation: Set up an automated workflow where any item tagged as "Approved" in Notion is automatically pulled into your next scheduled send. This system allows you to batch-process your curation, turning a complex task into a simple, repeatable process. You can learn more about the specifics of sending emails directly from your Notion workspace.

Pro Tip: Don't just list links. Add a short, insightful sentence or two explaining why each item is important. This personal analysis is your unique value proposition and what keeps subscribers coming back.

## 2. Educational/How-To Newsletter

The educational newsletter is one of the most effective formats for newsletters for building authority and trust. It focuses on teaching subscribers a specific skill, concept, or process through structured, step-by-step instruction. Instead of just reporting news, you are actively empowering your audience with actionable knowledge, positioning yourself as an indispensable expert.

This format creates deep, long-term engagement by providing tangible value. Subscribers don't just read your content; they learn from it and apply it. Newsletters from creators like Seth Godin and Pat Flynn of Smart Passive Income have built loyal followings by consistently delivering high-value lessons that help their readers grow professionally and personally.

### When to Use This Format

This format is perfect when your goal is to nurture leads, demonstrate expertise, or sell an info-product or service. It's ideal for coaches, consultants, software companies, and creators who want to build a relationship grounded in value. Use it to break down complex topics into digestible lessons, guiding your audience toward a specific outcome or understanding.

### Implementation with NotionSender

Notion is the perfect environment for structuring an educational series.

- Content Planning: Create a Notion database to outline your entire course or lesson series. Use properties to track the lesson number, topic, status (Draft, Ready, Sent), and send date.
- Reusable Templates: Design a "Lesson Template" within NotionSender. This template should include sections for an introduction, key learning objectives, the core content with step-by-step instructions, and a "homework" or action item.
- Feedback Loop: Create a system to capture reader questions and feedback directly into a separate Notion database. This feedback can fuel future content and help you refine your lessons. You can learn more about the different ways to use Notion to send emails and manage your content workflow.

Pro Tip: Structure your educational emails as a mini-course. Number your lessons (e.g., "Lesson 1 of 5: Mastering Subject Lines") to create a sense of progression and encourage subscribers to open every email so they don't miss a step.

 

## 3. Personal/Narrative Newsletter

The personal or narrative newsletter is one of the most intimate and connection-driven formats for newsletters. It shifts the focus from aggregation or promotion to authentic, first-person storytelling. This format builds a deep, parasocial relationship with subscribers by sharing personal experiences, reflections, and behind-the-scenes insights.

Instead of a formal, polished tone, it adopts a conversational, almost diary-like voice. Readers feel like they are getting a personal letter from a friend, not a marketing email. This approach fosters exceptional loyalty and trust. Creators like Anne Helen Petersen with Culture Study and the wave of writers on Substack have built entire careers on this model, proving that vulnerability and personal perspective are powerful currencies.

### When to Use This Format

This format is perfect for solo creators, thought leaders, coaches, and artists who want to build a strong personal brand. It excels when your unique perspective is the core product. Use it to share life lessons, document a creative process, or offer reflections on your industry. It's less about driving immediate sales and more about cultivating a dedicated community that will support your work long-term.

### Implementation with NotionSender

Notion is an ideal environment for nurturing a personal newsletter, turning abstract thoughts into structured content.

- Story Idea Database: Create a Notion database to serve as a "story bank." Capture fleeting thoughts, memories, and observations. Use tags like "Life Lesson," "Work Story," or "Reflection" to categorize ideas for future newsletters.
- Reader Relationship CRM: Set up a simple CRM in Notion to track interactions. When a reader replies with a personal story, you can log it to remember key details, fostering a genuine connection over time.
- Drafting in Templates: Develop a Notion template for your newsletter structure. Include sections for a personal opening, the main story, and a reflective closing question. This helps you consistently hit the right tone while batching your writing process in advance.

Pro Tip: Maintain a clear boundary. While vulnerability is key, you control the narrative. Decide in advance what aspects of your life are open for discussion and which remain private. Authenticity doesn't require total transparency.

## 4. Data-Driven/Analytics Newsletter

The data-driven newsletter is one of the most authoritative formats for newsletters. It establishes credibility by delivering original research, hard statistics, and insightful analysis. Instead of relying on opinion, this format centers on verifiable data, presented through charts, graphs, and concise storytelling to help subscribers make better, more informed decisions.

This format positions you as an indispensable resource for strategic thinkers and industry leaders. Readers subscribe not just for information but for proprietary insights they can’t get anywhere else. Publications like The Economist's data briefings and Adam Tooze's Chartbook have built devoted followings by consistently delivering high-signal, data-rich narratives that clarify complex topics.

### When to Use This Format

This format is ideal when your audience consists of analysts, executives, investors, or anyone whose role depends on making data-backed decisions. It works exceptionally well if you have access to proprietary data or the resources to conduct original research. Use it to establish deep expertise and create a high-value asset that is difficult for competitors to replicate.

### Implementation with NotionSender

A data-driven newsletter benefits immensely from a structured Notion backend to manage and analyze information.

- Data Repository: Create a Notion database to act as your central data library. Add properties to track data sources, collection dates, key metrics, and relevant categories. This creates a historical archive for future trend analysis.
- Templating for Consistency: Design a NotionSender template with dedicated blocks for charts, key takeaways, and methodology notes. This ensures every data story is presented clearly and consistently, building reader trust.
- Automated Insights: Connect your data sources to Notion using integrations or APIs. Set up alerts that trigger when certain metrics cross a threshold, which can then be automatically flagged for inclusion in your next newsletter, helping you find stories within the data. You can learn more about sending emails directly from your Notion workspace.

Pro Tip: Don't just present a chart and expect it to speak for itself. Always include a brief "So What?" section that explains the significance of the data and provides actionable context for your reader.

## 5. Product Update/Company Newsletter

The product update or company newsletter is one of the most critical formats for newsletters for any business with a tangible product or service. It's the direct line of communication for sharing feature releases, bug fixes, company milestones, and important organizational news. This format keeps your users engaged, informed, and invested in your journey.

This format is essential for maintaining transparency and managing customer expectations. When users see consistent progress and understand the 'why' behind changes, it builds trust and reduces churn. Companies like Slack, Notion, and Figma use this format exceptionally well to announce new features, turning routine updates into exciting events for their user base.

### When to Use This Format

This format is a must-have for SaaS companies, software developers, and any business that regularly updates its offerings. Use it to announce new features, share a product roadmap, communicate policy changes, or celebrate company achievements. It is also highly effective for keeping internal stakeholders and investors aligned with company progress.

### Implementation with NotionSender

Notion is the perfect single source of truth for all product developments, making it a powerful hub for your update newsletter.

- Content Capture: Create a central Notion database for all feature releases, bug fixes, and company news. Each entry can include details like release date, a summary of the change, relevant help-docs, and customer feedback.
- Templating: Design standardized templates in your NotionSender database for different types of announcements, such as "New Feature," "Bug Fix," or "Company Milestone." This ensures consistency in your messaging.
- Automation: Set up a view in your Notion database filtered for items marked "Ready for Announcement." NotionSender can automatically pull these items into your next scheduled update, ensuring you never miss communicating an important change. Pro Tip: Don't just announce what's new; explain the benefit. Frame every update around how it solves a customer's problem or improves their workflow. Including a short GIF or video demonstrating the new feature in action can dramatically increase adoption.

## 6. Weekly/Daily Briefing Newsletter

The daily or weekly briefing is one of the most habit-forming formats for newsletters. It delivers concise, time-sensitive information on a strict, predictable schedule, transforming your newsletter from a periodic email into an essential daily or weekly ritual. Its power lies in brevity and timeliness, giving subscribers the core intelligence they need to start their day or week fully informed.

This format builds immense loyalty by becoming an indispensable part of a subscriber's routine. Readers who value efficiency and staying ahead of the curve will open your email with the same regularity as their morning coffee. Iconic newsletters like Morning Brew, The Skimm, and Axios AM have built empires on this model by mastering the art of the quick, essential briefing.

### When to Use This Format

This format is perfect if your audience consists of busy professionals who need to stay informed but lack the time for deep dives. It is highly effective for industries with a rapid news cycle, such as tech, finance, or politics. Use this format to position your brand as an essential, timely source of information that respects your audience's time and attention.

- Templating: Build a master template in your NotionSender database with predefined sections (e.g., Top Story, Market Movers, Quick Bites). This creates a consistent structure that your readers will recognize and appreciate, making your content easy to scan.
- Scheduling and Automation: Use NotionSender's scheduling feature to queue up your briefings in advance. Set any Notion page with a "Ready to Send" status to automatically be scheduled for your daily 6 AM or weekly Monday morning slot. This automation guarantees consistent delivery, which is the cornerstone of this format's success.

Pro Tip: Your newsletter's value is directly tied to its consistency. Use Notion to pre-write and schedule at least one or two briefings in advance. This buffer protects your publishing schedule from unexpected disruptions and ensures you never miss a send.

## 7. Interactive/Engagement-Focused Newsletter

The interactive newsletter is one of the most dynamic formats for newsletters, transforming passive consumption into active participation. This format is designed to create a two-way dialogue with your audience by incorporating elements like polls, surveys, quizzes, and Q&A sections directly into the email. It moves beyond just broadcasting information to building a genuine community.

By inviting subscribers to contribute, you significantly boost engagement metrics and foster a stronger sense of belonging. Readers feel heard and valued, which makes them more invested in your content. Newsletters like Culture Study use reader questions to drive discussion, while others leverage polls and quizzes to make the experience more fun and memorable.

### When to Use This Format

This format is perfect when your primary goal is community building or gathering audience feedback. It's highly effective for creators, community managers, and brands who want to understand their subscribers' preferences, pain points, and opinions. Use it to generate user-driven content, validate ideas, or simply make your newsletter a more anticipated and engaging event in your readers' inboxes.

### Implementation with NotionSender

NotionSender is perfectly suited for managing the data generated by an interactive newsletter.

- Response Capture: Set up your interactive elements (e.g., a simple poll using linked text or a form) to feed responses directly into a dedicated Notion database. Use an integration or a tool like Zapier to automatically create a new entry for each submission.
- Content Templating: Create different Notion templates for various interactive segments like "Poll of the Week," "Reader Q&A," or "Weekly Quiz." This ensures your format is consistent and easy to deploy.
- Data Analysis: Once responses are collected in Notion, use its database features to sort, filter, and analyze the data. Identify trends and popular opinions to inform future content. You can even create a system to feature the best or most insightful reader responses in subsequent newsletters.

Pro Tip: Close the loop by sharing the results of polls or surveys in your next issue. This validates subscribers' participation and shows them that their input has a real impact, which can dramatically increase your open rates for future sends.

## 8. Industry News/Trend Monitoring Newsletter

The industry news and trend monitoring newsletter is one of the most valuable formats for newsletters for B2B audiences. It acts as a professional intelligence briefing, delivering targeted analysis of market shifts, regulatory updates, competitive moves, and emerging trends directly to your subscribers' inboxes. Instead of broad news, you provide deep, niche-specific insights that help readers stay ahead.

This format positions you as an indispensable industry analyst. Your audience, composed of decision-makers and professionals, comes to depend on your newsletter to inform their strategy and navigate a complex landscape. Newsletters like Retail Dive and Healthcare Brew have mastered this by providing specialized intelligence that general news outlets simply cannot match, making their content essential reading.

### When to Use This Format

This format is perfect when your audience needs to make informed business decisions based on timely industry information. It's highly effective for B2B companies, consultants, and analysts looking to build a reputation as a foremost expert in a specific vertical. Use it to attract a high-value, professional audience that sees your content as a competitive advantage.

### Implementation with NotionSender

Pro Tip: Archive past newsletters and curated articles within Notion. Over time, this creates a searchable historical database of industry trends, allowing you to connect current events to past patterns and provide much deeper, more insightful analysis.

## 9. Community/Member Newsletter

The community or member newsletter is one of the most relationship-centric formats for newsletters. Its primary goal is not acquisition but retention and engagement. It’s designed to foster a sense of belonging among an existing group, like paying subscribers, course students, or members of a private group.

This format strengthens community bonds by delivering exclusive content, member spotlights, and inside information that makes recipients feel valued. Instead of broadcasting to a wide audience, you're nurturing a core tribe. Newsletters from platforms like Patreon, Substack (for paying members), and Mighty Networks excel at this by creating an intimate, members-only dialogue that reinforces the value of being part of the group.

### When to Use This Format

This format is essential if you run a membership site, a paid community, a subscription service, or any business model that relies on long-term customer loyalty. Use it to reduce churn, encourage participation, and transform passive customers into active brand advocates. It's the perfect vehicle for sharing user-generated content, celebrating member milestones, and providing behind-the-scenes updates.

Pro Tip: Make your members the heroes of the newsletter. Regularly feature member spotlights, success stories, or projects. This not only provides social proof but also encourages deeper engagement as members see their peers being celebrated.

## 10. Resource/Tool Recommendation Newsletter

The resource or tool recommendation newsletter is one of the most directly valuable formats for newsletters for a niche audience. This format moves beyond simple curation by providing in-depth reviews, comparisons, and practical use cases for specific products, software, templates, or resources. It positions you as a trusted advisor who helps readers make better purchasing and implementation decisions.

This format builds immense trust and authority. Subscribers see you as an unbiased expert who has done the heavy lifting of testing and vetting options, saving them time and money. Newsletters like Sidebar (for design tools) or various Notion template round-ups have built dedicated followings by consistently delivering high-quality, actionable recommendations that solve specific problems for their readers.

### When to Use This Format

This format is perfect when your audience is actively looking for solutions to improve their workflow, productivity, or business operations. It’s highly effective for monetizing your newsletter through affiliate marketing or sponsored placements, as the content is inherently commercial. Use this format if you enjoy testing new products and can provide genuine, detailed evaluations that go beyond surface-level features.

## Why is good email design essential for driving engagement?

Regardless if you’re sending out newsletters, promotional emails, transactional emails, or other types of emails, as part of an email marketing strategy, the design of the messages sent can make or break your email performance.

Why is this the case? Well, you see, email design goes hand in hand with the effectiveness of email marketing campaigns and the amount of engagement they receive.

So, if an email is well-designed, it will be visually appealing, responsive, and all other things that facilitate a great user experience. And if an email recipient has a good user experience, chances are they will engage with the email and take the desired action.

How will you know if you nailed your email design? Besides how the email looks visually to you and your team, the following performance metrics should be a good indicator:

- Deliverability rate: The number of emails delivered divided by the total number of emails sent multiplied by 100
- Open rate: The number of unique email opens divided by the number of emails delivered multiplied by 100
- Click-through rate: The number of unique clicks on links within an email divided by the number of emails delivered multiplied by 100.
- Conversion rate: The number of conversions generated from an email campaign divided by the number of unique clicks on the email’s call-to-action (CTA) multiplied by 100.

## What are the top characteristics of a well-designed newsletter?

When it comes to creating your email newsletter, you don’t just write and send it impulsively. First, you learn what makes a newsletter well-designed, among other things, and then you invest time and effort into planning and bringing it to life.

Here are some well-designed newsletter characteristics to keep in mind:

### It’s readable

Newsletters should be a quick and easy way to get information, so if a newsletter becomes difficult to read, it will lose its appeal and effectiveness and won’t engage the audience.

To avoid this, in every newsletter, include plenty of white space, clear and concise content, a well-structured layout, appropriate font and font size, headers, subheaders, and proper formatting.

Source: Envato Elements

### Tells a story

Your newsletter content should, first and foremost, make sense. And once you have that covered, you should make sure it has a storytelling aspect to it.

You can achieve this by adding a narrative structure, captivating introduction, conversational language, emotional appeal, real-life examples, visuals, continuity, and cohesion. Paragraph generator is a useful tool as it helps you generate narrative style paragraphs or you can turn your existing content in similar structure. After that, you can use the content right away!

Source: Envato Elements

### Focuses on the audience

Like all content created for your brand or business, a newsletter should be valuable and beneficial to your audience. This way, it will establish trust, build relationships, and become a trusted source of information and insights.

Relevant, informative, personalized, and actionable content is what your newsletter should feature if you want it to be truly audience-focused.

Also, to catch the reader’s attention, you can adjust your writing style and use first and second-person pronouns in your copy.

Source: Envato Elements

### Includes CTAs

What action do you want your audience to take? Maybe read new product announcements or purchase a product on your eCommerce store? Regardless of what the action is, to push the audience toward it, create your CTA button so it’s eye-catching and easy to understand.

Source: Envato Elements

## What are the five elements of a well-designed newsletter?

With the characteristics of a well-designed newsletter out of the way, now it’s time we cover its basic elements. These elements are:

### 1. Attention-grabbing subject line

The email subject line is the first thing that your recipients will see, so it’s crucial to make it interesting enough to encourage them to open your email. A good subject line should be concise, informative, and create a sense of urgency or excitement, just like this one from Crate and Barrel:

### 2. Engaging content

Sparking curiosity, evoking emotions and participation, as well as building a loyal audience are just some of the things engaging content can do.

To turn your content from a boring block of text to an engaging piece of writing, you should incorporate interactive elements within your visually-appealing design, ask thought-provoking questions, nail your storytelling and a conversational tone, as well as add some personalized recommendations.

If you need ideas for engaging content forms, case studies, customer success stories, quizzes, how-tos, BTS content, updates, and so on, are always a smart choice. You may use services like EssayPro or others to help you write high-quality, engaging content to attract attention and interest readers.

### 3. Great layout

What’s the point of crafting great content if reading and navigating it is a struggle? For this reason, it’s crucial you apply design principles to lay out all the elements of the newsletter in a way that allows a balance between whitespace, headings, and organized sections of content. Not only will this be visually appealing, but it will also be easily scannable.

Another thing to keep in mind is your font choice and color palette choice, as well as the visuals you go for, as this affects how effectively your message is being communicated and the reading experience in general. In case you see something attractive from your competitors, you can now clone their colors. If you can work with Figma and want to integrate your designs into your website or newsletter, you just need to transform your Figma designs into HTML online.

### 4. Clear call-to-action

A clear CTA encourages readers to take a specific action. This could be visiting your website, making a purchase, signing up for a service, or following your social media pages.

When coming up with your CTA, pay attention to how clear and concise the language you are using is and how prominently placed the button is. Other things to think about include the button’s size and color.

### 5. Personalization

Personalization is achieved through the use of the recipient’s name, location, and other relevant information and aims to build a relationship with your audience and increase engagement.

And if you’re thinking about whether skipping on personalization is possible, the answer is “no”. Why? It’s simple!

People nowadays are constantly bombarded with emails on top of emails from all kinds of businesses, and any non-personalized attempt at communication, be it a company newsletter or something else, might come across as mass emailing or, even worse, spam. Your newsletter should serve as an electronic business card, making each recipient feel individually addressed and valued.

## How do you structure a newsletter?

Email elements are like puzzle pieces, meaning they should be put together carefully. Still, there are many ways to structure a newsletter, and how you should structure yours will depend on your goals.

As a general example, here is the structure of a traditional newsletter:

- Newsletter header: This typically includes your newsletter’s title and logo. Along with this, the header may also include a title or number for the specific newsletter issue.
- Introduction: Here is where you tell your readers what to expect in the newsletter content. Do keep in mind that you’ll have new and old email list contacts reading, so the newsletter introduction will play an important role in making sure nobody is confused.
- Core content and its sections: We’ve covered core content a bit earlier in the article, so we won’t go back into the same topic again. The only thing we will note is to break up the piece of content that is your newsletter into a few sections once it’s written to help with readability.
- CTAs: Depending on your goals, you may have multiple CTAs sprinkled throughout your core content. In other words, sticking to one CTA towards the end of your newsletter is, of course, not a must.
- Footer: Last but not least is the spot where you put things like contact information and links to your website and social media. Here is also where you should include an unsubscribe link in order to be compliant with data protection laws and regulations.

## Steps for designing a newsletter

### Planning the newsletter

The first step in designing a newsletter is, you guessed it, planning the content and overall structure of the newsletter. Here you will make decisions on some “creative” details, such as the tone and style of writing, as well as some “basic” details, like the sending frequency of the newsletter.

Take as much time as you can to complete this step, as a well-planned newsletter can help establish brand authority, increase engagement, boost conversions, and reap the other benefits that come with newsletter sending.

For some help, watch our video on the 10 newsletter content ideas for achieving different business goals:

### Deciding on your target audience

A target audience is a specific group of people that you want to target with your newsletter. This could be past customers, potential customers, or just a specific demographic.

Once you know who this audience is, you can create content that is highly relevant and engaging specifically for them, and thus, increase the likelihood of conversions.

### Choosing the appropriate software for your newsletter

Email-sending software should allow you to create, distribute, and track the performance of newsletters. And when it comes to options, there are plenty available, each with different features and pricing structures. Just keep in mind to choose something that meets your specific needs and budget.

### Deciding on the conversion action for the newsletter

For each of your newsletters, you’ll want to have a specific action (a conversion action) that your readers should complete during or after reading your newsletter. This could be purchasing, signing up, or simply visiting your website. Creating a landing page that effectively converts visitors into sales can have a significant impact.

By clearly defining a desired conversion action, you can tailor your newsletter layout and content to encourage readers to take that action.

### Choosing a layout

For your layout, you can choose to use an email newsletter template and then customize it or come up with one from scratch using code or a drag-and-drop editor.

When deciding on the layout, go for something visually appealing that will also present your content in the best way possible while directing readers toward your CTA.

Still, do keep in mind that the only way you’ll know if a specific layout will work for you is by putting it through some tests, such as A/B tests, preview tests, etc.

### Creating good content and personalizing it

Content creation is a process different for each company, and each writer within it, so we can’t give many pointers on it. If you have multiple writers in your team, consider making use of content approval software so you can continuously review, comment and approve content.

### Scheduling

When you schedule your newsletter to go out can also impact the engagement it receives. So, consider the time zones your audience covers, and based on that as well as the recommended times and days for newsletter sending, pick something that will work best.

We should note that your sending schedule is also an aspect you should test if you want to achieve optimal email newsletter performance, as your target audience might prefer receiving emails on days and times you were not expecting.

### Testing

Even though your newsletter might seem like it turned out perfect, this is rarely the case, especially on the first try. To spot and remove any errors, you’ll need to test your newsletter with proper email testing tools that can inspect and debug everything from the HTML email code, content, email headers, SMTP transaction info, mobile device responsiveness, email client (Outlook, Gmail, etc.) rendering, and more.

Other types of testing you can do are A/B testing, where you create different versions of the same email and compare their performance, testing different audience segments, testing different sending times, and so on.

### Tracking results and making improvements

Tracking your results and analyzing them is the only surefire way to improve things for the better. So, after each email you send, keep an eye on its performance metrics to see what content, design, etc. resonates with your audience the most and make adjustments accordingly.

## Email newsletter design tips and best practices

### Use high-quality images and graphics

While a quality, engaging copy is super important, images, graphic designs, and even GIFs keep things visually interesting and can provide essential context for your readers.

For that, you can utilize graphic asset libraries, which offer everything from location pin icons ideal for travel agencies to showcase exciting destinations to star graphics to highlight best-selling products in your newsletter.

So, in every newsletter you send, include high-quality stock images or original ones if you have them.

Also, at all costs, avoid using pixelated, irrelevant or blurry images, as these can distract the reader, leave a bad impression, and pull attention away from the information you’re communicating.

Using high-quality stock images or original ones can make designing your newsletter much easier and leave you with a beautiful email like this one from The New York Times.

Source: The New York Times Wellness Newsletter

### Don’t overdo it

Going over the top with your newsletter design can be tempting, but a minimalist approach can often be more effective and less distracting. Just think how much more readable a simple newsletter is compared to one with a flashy design.

Through simplicity, you allow readers to focus, thus improving engagement and the understanding of the key messaging.

### Make your content accessible

Having a newsletter with content accessible to people with disabilities can help you reach a wider audience and send more traffic to your product pages and landing pages.

Here are just a few things you should keep in mind regarding content accessibility:

- Typically, sans-serif, web-safe fonts are best when it comes to font legibility. So, use them instead of complex typography and try to stick to a font size greater than 12pt.
- Using a color scheme with low contrast can make it difficult (or even impossible) for folks with vision disabilities to read or view content. To avoid this, use a color contrast detector and ensure you’re using a color scheme that provides sufficient contrast between text and background colors.
- When it comes to images and logos, make sure to include alt-text that accurately describes them when incorporated into the content.

Source: Feedly Newsletter

### Keep an eye on trends

While email best practices tend to stay the same, email marketing trends are ever-changing. And if you want to have your newsletter stand out from the rest, keeping an eye on the top trends as well as incorporating them into your email design is a must.

## Summary

If done right, newsletters can have a massive positive impact on the relationship with your audience. However, you have to be aware of the effort that goes into creating the best email newsletter, starting from defining goals to perfecting the user experience.

Fortunately, with this step-by-step guide, you’ll know how to design a newsletter in no time!

## What Is an Email Newsletter?

An email newsletter is a regular email that goes out weekly, biweekly, or monthly to keep subscribers updated. Instead of pushing one single offer, it packs several small pieces of content into a single send.

- That’s the main difference between a newsletter and a regular marketing email.
- A marketing email usually asks for one thing: buy this, sign up for that.
- A newsletter mixes a few things, such as a main story, a couple of extra links, maybe a product update or an upcoming event.

## What Makes a Newsletter’s HTML Actually Good?

Good newsletter HTML loads fast, looks right in every inbox, and doesn’t fall apart on a phone. 55–60% of all emails are now opened on mobile devices; that’s why most non-mobile-friendly emails get deleted within seconds.

Here’s where most newsletter layouts fall apart, and how each example below avoids it:

| Problem | Why It Happens | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Layout collapses in Outlook | Outlook renders emails with the Microsoft Word engine. | Use nested HTML tables with inline styles instead of CSS Grid or Flexbox. |
| Blank space where an image should be | Many inboxes block images by default. | Add real, descriptive alt text to every image. |
| Text hard to read in dark mode | Transparent PNGs or light-only text colors invert unpredictably. | Test dark mode directly. Don’t assume it inherits your light theme. |
| Wasted first line in the inbox | Preview text defaults to “view in browser”. | Write your own preview text that adds value to the subject line. |
| Multi-column section looks improper on phones | No mobile-specific stacking rule. | Force a single-column layout below 600px. |

Take a two-column “story + image” block as an example.

## What’s the Ideal Width for an HTML Email Newsletter?

600 to 800 pixels is the ideal width. That’s narrow enough to avoid horizontal scrolling on mobile and wide enough to look intentional on desktop.

Screens used to only support that size, but that reason doesn’t really hold up anymore since most screens and email clients today handle widths well beyond 600px. The safest way to know your ideal width is still to test your own email across the clients your subscribers actually use.

To stay safe, keep your newsletter’s width somewhere between 600 and 650px.

Not sure how to land on the right number? Postcards, our email builder, builds templates at 600px by default. Push it to about 700px if you want more room, or go wider once you’ve tested it properly.

## Should Newsletters Be Built With Tables or CSS?

Use HTML tables, not modern layout tools like Grid or Flexbox. Outlook renders emails through the Microsoft Word engine, and Word doesn’t understand a lot of modern CSS. That mismatch is the most common reason a newsletter looks perfect in Gmail and improper in Outlook.

A two-column layout built with Flexbox, for example, can stack into two separate full-width blocks in Outlook instead of sitting side by side, because Outlook ignores the Flexbox code entirely. Tables don’t have that problem.

## 12 Best Email Newsletter Examples by Category

Every example below leads with what it does well, then gives you one concrete layout or code detail you can reuse.

### 1. Brew Markets

Hundreds of thousands of people start their morning with Brew Markets because it delivers the day’s market news in a few minutes.

- Preview up top: a short greeting followed by a bulleted “in today’s newsletter” summary, so readers know what’s coming before they scroll.
- Numbers in a table: a market snapshot table for exact figures like stock prices and interest rates.
- Story blocks: a headline, an image, and a short summary with bolded sub-points.
- Sponsored content, clearly marked: it gets its own background tint so no one mistakes it for editorial content.
- Up or down at a glance: the “Movers & Groovers” section swaps the table for small green and red dot icons, which read faster than numbers do.

The whole email holds together because every block uses the same thin dividers and typeface, even as the content format changes block to block.

That consistency is the real lesson: pick the visual format based on what the reader needs to do with the number.

### 2. Notion

Notion’s newsletter solves a problem a lot of product emails ignore: not every reader wants to read a guide when they’d rather watch one.

- A 2×2 grid of short video guides for people who learn faster by watching.
- One primary CTA button behind the main pitch.
- A separate boxed option, “Prefer to read a guide?”, with its own button for people who want text instead.

The lesson here is simple. Don’t force everyone into the same learning format. Offering a five-minute written guide next to a set of short videos costs very little, and it means neither group has to settle for a format that doesn’t fit them.

### 3. Webflow

Webflow’s newsletter has a lot to say in one email, and it manages that without turning into a wall of buttons.

- A bold, colorful hero built from small UI-style tags.
- One intro paragraph and one CTA button.
- A six-item feature grid where each item gets its own color, a linked title, and a short description instead of its own button.
- A second CTA and an event callout to close things out.

Only two things in this whole email get a full button: the main pitch and the event invite. Everything in that feature grid earns just a linked title and a line of text.

That restraint is worth copying. When you have six things to mention, giving all six a button dilutes the important ones.

### 4. Litmus

Litmus barely uses design at all, and that’s exactly the point.

- A centered logo, one headline, one short paragraph.
- A plain bulleted list of three linked resources.
- One closing CTA link.

There’s no grid, no color palette, and no hero image competing for attention here, and the email is better for it. When you only point people toward a handful of resources, a plain list of links is faster to build than a designed grid, and it’s faster for the reader to scan too.

### 5. Grammarly

Grammarly’s newsletter turns your own writing habits into the pitch, which is a smart use of data the company already has.

- A streak counter up top.
- Three stat blocks (productivity, accuracy, vocabulary), each compared against other users as a percentile.
- A tone breakdown and a running total of words analyzed.
- An upgrade pitch built from that same usage data: the exact count of advanced suggestions the free plan holds back (3,408, in this case).

That last detail is what makes the upgrade pitch better. Instead of a generic list of Plus features, Grammarly shows the specific number of suggestions you personally missed last week.

A number tied to your own account is much harder to ignore than a bullet list of hypothetical benefits.

### 6. Figma

Figma had five features to announce in one email, and it solved the organization problem with color.

- A bold, oversized hero announcing the news.
- The same repeating pattern for each feature: a two-tone color pill label (Figma Sites, Figma Make, Figma Buzz), one line about the benefit, a text-link CTA, and a screenshot underneath.
- Each section’s colors match its own pill.

The layout stays exactly the same for every feature, and only the color changes. That does two things at once: readers can tell the sections apart at a glance, but the email still feels like one announcement instead of five separate emails stapled together.

### 7. HubSpot

HubSpot’s Data Sync announcement email numbers the benefits instead of listing them.

- A short, personalized greeting and a two-sentence intro to the feature.
- A bold subheading (“With data sync, you now have access to:”) followed by three numbered points, each with a circular number badge, a bold sub-title, and a short paragraph.
- Two learning links for people who want more depth: a short video lesson and an interactive demo.
- One final CTA button.
- Numbering the three capabilities instead of bulleting them sounds like a small choice, but it changes how the reader thinks about the feature.

A bulleted list reads like a spec sheet, whereas a numbered one reads like a sequence of things you get, which is easier to remember and easier to bring up later.

### 8. Canva

Canva’s newsletter promotes one big feature and four smaller ones underneath it, and it treats those two jobs differently on purpose.

- A bold headline and short paragraph for the main feature (video editing), backed by one CTA.
- A full-width visual banner that reinforces the same feature.
- A 2×2 grid of secondary features (templates, free assets, the editor, collaboration), where every item gets its own full button.

Every item in that secondary grid is a genuinely different tool, not four related links to the same idea, so each one earns a full button instead of a linked title.

Give a full button to something the reader can click on as its own destination, and save the plain link for things that are closer to footnotes.

### 9. Loom

Loom’s monthly recap leads with an outcome and that one choice does a lot of work.

- A headline stat framed around time saved rather than raw activity: “You eliminated 2 meetings.”
- A breakdown of videos created, received, and watched.
- A customer testimonial from Intercom about saving 12 days of a sales manager’s time.
- A small carousel of real videos other users made, right inside the recap.

Two meetings sound like a small number until you remember what a meeting actually costs in a day. Pair that outcome with someone else’s testimonial in the same email, and you turn your own usage stats into social proof at the same time, without needing a separate case study.

### 10. foodpanda

foodpanda’s promo email personalizes the email (not only the greeting) and that’s the part worth copying.

- A personalized greeting with the subscriber’s first name worked into the copy.
- A “recommended for you” grid of six restaurants, each with its own live discount badge instead of one blanket offer repeated six times.
- A coupon code inside a dashed, ticket-style border, so it reads like something to tear off and use.

Most promo emails personalize the greeting and stop there. foodpanda carries that same idea into the product grid, so each restaurant shows its own live discount instead of the same generic banner over and over.

Six different offers feel more relevant than one offer copied six times, even when the total discount is similar.

### 11. Kamran Ahmed

Kamran Ahmed’s newsletter reads like an email from a person because it is one.

- A first-name greeting and a casual, first-person update from Kamran himself.
- An embedded mini tool right inside the email with a “What can I help you learn?” input box along with Course, Guide, and Roadmap options.
- Short sections underneath for each new feature, each with its own button.
- A real sign-off, “Kamran, roadmap.sh,” instead of a company name.

The embedded tool is the standout choice here. Most product emails just show a screenshot of a feature and ask you to click through to try it. This one lets you start using the tool from inside the email itself, which removes a full step between seeing the feature and trying it.

### 12. Semrush

Semrush’s tooltip email is structured like a lesson plan.

- A “Use case” line explaining the problem it solves.
- An “Output” line showing what you’ll get.
- A product screenshot.
- A numbered “Your turn” list, four simple steps with circular number badges, that shows exactly how to do it yourself.
- One closing CTA button, a short FAQ box, and a quick emoji feedback rating.

Use case, then output, then steps, in that order, means the reader knows what they’re getting before you ask them to do anything. That order matters more than it looks like it should. A numbered list of steps is also just easier to act on than the same instructions written as a paragraph.

## FAQs

### What’s the difference between a subject line and preheader text?

The subject line is the first thing someone sees in their inbox list. The preheader is the short preview text right after it, and if you don’t set it deliberately, most clients default to pulling in your first line of body text or a “view in browser” link.

### Does dark mode change my newsletter automatically, or do I have to design for it?

Some email clients auto-invert colors for dark mode, which can make light text disappear or backgrounds look wrong in ways you didn’t intend. It’s safer to set dark-mode-friendly colors deliberately than to let the client guess.

### Should every content block have its own CTA?

Yes. People read newsletters in short scroll bursts, and a reader who stops at any single block should still see a clear next action instead of finding one CTA at the very bottom.

### Should I include social media icons in my newsletter?

Only if you’re active enough on those platforms to make the click worth it; otherwise, a row of icons linking to inactive accounts adds clutter without giving subscribers anywhere useful to go.

You can choose from save templates, fully designed options, basic layouts, start from scratch, use your own HTML, or reuse a recent email. For now, select basic layout. The page will reload and show you a set of simple layout templates. Take a moment to browse through them and pick one that fits your content structure. When you found one you like, hover over it and click apply. The editor will open with that layout ready to customize. Inside the editor, your template appears on the right and the editing tools are on the left. On the left panel, you'll see blocks like text, images, buttons, and more. You can drag and drop these blocks directly onto your template to build out your newsletter. You'll also see sections for columns and pre-built layouts if you want a more complex design. At the top of the left panel, click on styles to adjust the overall look of your email. Here you can customize things like the background color, default text styles, link colors, button designs, dividers, images, and logo settings. This helps you match your newsletter to your brand. To edit any existing block in the template, simply click on it. A properties panel will open on the left with tabs such as content, styles, visibility, or code depending on the block type. Use these tabs to change text, swap images, adjust spacing, and control how the block appears. On the selected block in the preview, you'll notice small icons that let you move, duplicate, or delete that block, which is helpful for rearranging your layout quickly. Once you're happy with the design and content, go to the top right and click save and exit. Wait for the page to reload. You'll now see a summary screen for your email campaign. Here you'll review and finalize key settings. In the to section, choose the audience or segment you want to send the newsletter to. You can also specify who not to send it to. And there's an option to personalize the recipient field, which is useful if you want to include your subscribers name. Next, check the from section. Make sure the sender name and email address are what you want your subscribers to see in their inbox. Then, move to the subject section. Enter a clear and engaging subject line and add preview text if you'd like a short summary to appear next to the subject in the inbox. Both of these can have a big impact on your open rates. Anytime you adjust one of these sections, remember to click save within that accordion before collapsing it so your changes aren't lost. When everything looks good and you're ready to go, click send in the top right corner. A confirmation pop-up will appear to make sure you're certain about sending. Click send now to confirm. Newsletters can come in a variety of styles, subjects, formats and layouts, but following the steps below on how to write a newsletter correctly should give you the starting ammunition you will need to pull the trigger and get your newsletter to hit its target. This is how to write a newsletter perfectly:

## 1. Your first point is crucial

Get your most compelling point across succinctly in the first sentence.

## 2. Be an expert

Write about what you know, or what your company excels in.

## 3. Make it interesting

The main deciding factor in the success or failure of a newsletter campaign is the written content itself. It just isn’t enough to use proper English grammar and an extensive vocabulary. The newsletter needs to be easy to read, interesting, relatable and relevant to what’s going on in today’s society.

## 4. Short and sweet

If your newsletter articles tend to be overwritten and long, the reader won’t hesitate to put them down and brush them aside. Smart, witty and intelligent shorter articles will draw the reader in and make them more likely to pick up your newsletters a second time.

## 5. Personalize your content

When making email newsletters you usually have the advantage of knowing the reader’s name, as well as other identifying information and even their interests. ActivePersonalization from ActiveTrail email newsletter software utilizes this information to allow you to personalize both text and images, making your newsletter more personal to each reader.

## 6. Think about your aesthetic design

Our species as a whole is a very visual breed of animal. When designing your newsletter format, keep in mind that you must attract the reader at first with the initial look. It is said to not judge a book by its cover, yet we do this on a daily basis. ActiveTrail’s user-friendly newsletter editor has this covered. If an eye-catching picture or font attracts the reader right away then they’ll pick it up to see what content it has to offer inside.

## 7. Use bullet points

Get your point across quickly and succinctly. Studies show that users only fully read an average of 19% of the text in newsletters, and 35% of the time only scan a newsletter for the salient points. Bullet points are also the perfect format for any data or surveys that you want to include.

## 8. Stick to the topic

Many people who begin writing a newsletter tend to not have an exact direction in mind of where they’re going, and the end product is a jumbled up mess of a read. If it’s a newsletter in regards to a new business you’re promoting, make sure that all topics inside are relatable to the business.

## 9. Proofread

Proofread and then proofread again. Silly overlooked mistakes can cause a newsletter to seem unprofessional and just downright amateur.

## 10. Enjoy your writing

Finally, when asking yourself how to write a newsletter, remember the steps above – but have fun creating it. The amount of effort and energy that’s put into the project will definitely shine through. Be creative, be thoughtful and a little humor never hurts.

## Summary
Across the 2024–2026 guidance in the provided sources, the most consistent levers of a successful newsletter are format discipline, scannable structure, and clear calls to action. Practically, that means choosing a repeatable HTML template, opening with a focused story or promise, delivering content in discrete blocks with one action each, and using platform-native templates and workflows to launch and iterate. The sources emphasize design quality and format choice, but they do not provide hard-and-fast numbers for ideal length, cadence, or growth tactics.

## Key Findings
1) Format and structure are primary drivers of engagement; picking a format (e.g., single-topic vs. multi-block roundup) is as important as the content itself [1].  
2) High-performing newsletters share: a repeatable HTML template and one clear action per content block (useful guardrails for both single-topic and roundup issues) [3].  
3) Effective design is essential and should be readable, tell a story, focus on the audience, and include clear CTAs; a step-by-step design workflow is provided [2].  
4) Formatting matters; Mailchimp provides formatting tips and templates to get started and refine layout over time [8].  
5) Opening an issue with a clear story/promise aligns with “tells a story” and “audience focus,” then moving into action-oriented blocks supports engagement [2][3].  
6) A practical section order synthesized from the sources: concise opener (story/promise) → scannable content blocks (each with a single action) → primary CTA → closing note; use a consistent HTML template to enforce this order issue-to-issue [2][3][8].  
7) Designed HTML layouts are emphasized; sources highlight templates/design guidance, while no source presents head-to-head performance data versus plain-text emails [2][3][8].  
8) Platform setup: a 2026 Mailchimp tutorial shows the current flow—log in → Campaigns (left nav) → Create (top-right) → proceed with campaign setup—use this to launch and iterate [5].  
9) Getting started: step-by-step beginner walkthroughs exist for standing up a newsletter in general and in 2026 specifically, useful for first-time creators [4][7].  
10) Not covered with traceable specifics: exact issue length, sending rhythm, named “best-in-class” brand breakdowns, and concrete list-growth playbooks; the sources do not supply verifiable numbers or brand teardowns here [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].

## Detail

Section order that works (and why)
- Opener that “tells a story” and centers the reader’s benefit: The design guidance emphasizes readability and storytelling focused on the audience; use a short opening that frames what the reader will get and why it matters before you ask for action [2].  
- Scannable content blocks with a single action each: Designmodo’s 2026 guidance notes that the best newsletters keep one clear action per block and use a repeatable HTML template. This imposes hierarchy, prevents overload, and maps naturally to either a single deep-dive (one main block) or a curated roundup (several blocks) [3].  
- Clear CTAs: Calls to action are explicitly listed as a core element of effective newsletter design; place them where the decision is made—within or just after each block, and include a primary CTA for the issue [2].  
- Consistent template: Use one repeatable HTML template so readers recognize structure and can scan faster; Mailchimp provides formatting tips/templates to implement this, and Designmodo frames the template as a shared trait of top performers [3][8].

How to open an issue (step-by-step technique)
- Step 1: State the promise in a sentence or two—what new value this issue delivers. This follows the “tells a story” and “focuses on the audience” guidance [2].  
- Step 2: Transition immediately to the first action-oriented block. Keep the block singular in purpose (“one clear action”) and make the CTA explicit [3].  
- Step 3: If using multiple blocks, maintain the same micro-structure per block (title → 1–3 tight sentences → one CTA), preserving readability and scannability as emphasized in the design tutorial and formatting tips [2][8].  
- Step 4: Close with a concise summary or sign-off and one primary CTA (e.g., reply, share, or try the featured resource), aligning to “includes CTAs” and “focuses on the audience” [2].

Single-topic vs roundup formats
- Both work; your format choice is a “silent driver of engagement,” per the 2026 formats overview. Select the structure that best matches your goal for a given issue: depth (single-topic) or breadth (roundup) [1].  
- For single-topic issues: Lean into storytelling and readability (the “tells a story” guidance), using a single, well-developed block and a clear primary CTA [2][3].  
- For roundup issues: Use multiple discrete blocks, each with one clear action (Designmodo’s pattern), and a consistent layout so readers can quickly scan and choose what’s relevant [3][8].

- The sources stress readability, scannability, and clear CTAs rather than a fixed word count or scroll length. No source here provides a traceable numeric benchmark (e.g., words, links, or read-time) [2][3][8].
